title: Japan approves foreign resident visa renewal fee increases of up to 967 percent, starts soon
description: Fee for permanent residency jumps 1,900 percent. At a cabinet meeting held on the morning of August 25, the Japanese government approved a measure significantly raising the mandatory fees foreign nationals must pay when renewing or extending their Japanese residency visas, including those seeking permanent residency in the country. Under the current pricing structure, foreign […]
content:
Fee for permanent residency jumps 1,900 percent.

At a cabinet meeting held on the morning of August 25, the Japanese government approved a measure significantly raising the mandatory fees foreign nationals must pay when renewing or extending their Japanese residency visas, including those seeking permanent residency in the country.

Under the current pricing structure, foreign residents of Japan pay a fee of 6,000 yen (US$38) when renewing their residency permit or changing its status, such as transitioning from a student visa to a working visa, or from a working visa to a spousal visa following marriage to a Japanese citizen. That flat rate will be ending, and in its place will be a series of much higher, swiftly increasing prices depending on the length of visa being applied for.

● 3 months or less: 10,000 yen (67 percent increase over current price)
● 3-6 months: 18,000 yen (200 percent increase)
● 6 months-1 year: 25,000 yen (317 percent increase)
● 1 year exactly: 33,000 yen (450 percent increase)
● 1-3 years: 48,000 yen (700 percent increase)
● 3-5 years: 64,000 yen (967 percent increase)
● More than 5 years: 75,000 yen (1,150 percent increase)

The increase is even larger for those applying for permanent residency in Japan, for which the fee will jump from its current 10,000 yen to 200,000 yen, a 1,900 percent increase.

▼ This fan formed by 10,000-yen bills still isn’t enough to pay the new permanent residency fee.

The higher fees are part of a continuing trend for the Japanese government. This past June, the decision was made to increase visa fees for travelers from countries requiring one to enter Japan by 400 percent, which was followed up by the July announcement that the departure tax travelers must pay when flying out of Japan will triple.

The increase in residency visa fees comes at a time of complex, arguably distorted perceptions by many Japanese people regarding the financial status of foreigners in Japan. The weak yen has resulted in a surge of foreign tourists visiting the country, many of whom are enthusiastically enjoying sightseeing, restaurant dining, and other luxuries that are becoming increasingly out of reach for Japan’s middle and lower-earning households as inflation surges and wages for many remain stagnant. The exchange rate is also making it easier than ever before for foreign nationals to leverage their home country savings into purchasing homes and real estate in Japan, either for personal use or to convert to Airbnb-style vacation rental properties, fueling anxieties that yen-wealthy foreigners will drive up prices for housing. Combined, these factors make it easy to perceive, or paint, foreigners as uniformly financially well-off and benefitting from being on the opposite side of the coin from Japanese locals in the current economic climate.

What often gets overlooked, or is conveniently ignored by politicians looking to curry favor with their voting (i.e. Japanese citizen) constituents, is that the economic conditions that are adversely affecting the average Japanese citizen are having the same effects on the vast majority of Japan’s preexisting foreign resident population. The foreign convenience store clerk, English teacher at a Japanese high school, or study abroad program participant who found an office job with a Japanese company and stayed in the country are all getting paid in yen, so they’re not at all living high on the hog these days. It’s hard to say whether executing such massive increases in residency visa fees at a time when so many are already dealing with tighter finances would be better described as ignorant or insensitive, but it’s definitely somewhere on that spectrum.

It’s not like the Japanese government is giving foreign residents much time to sort out how they’re going to manage these higher fees, either. Again, the new pricing structure was announced on August 25, and it will go into effect for renewal and permanent residency applications starting October 1.

At the August 25 meeting, the cabinet also said that measures will be taken to allow for reductions to the new fees for foreign residents judged to be facing financial hardships. They don’t appear to have gotten around to figuring out what the qualifying factors will be, how reductions can be requested, or how much the fees will be reduced, but surely those are top priorities for them…right?

Source: Nitele News

title: Starbucks Japan adds new Customisation Bar to stores, with free ways to hack your food and drink orders
description: New bar helps to create up to 5.27 million possible combinations. Starbucks has been leaning into its customisations recently, offering suggestions on how to hack new limited-edition releases and exploring new ways for customers to personalise their drinks. Now the chain is taking things up a notch by introducing a new “My Customisation Bar” at […]
content:
New bar helps to create up to 5.27 million possible combinations.

Starbucks has been leaning into its customisations recently, offering suggestions on how to hack new limited-edition releases and exploring new ways for customers to personalise their drinks.

Now the chain is taking things up a notch by introducing a new “My Customisation Bar” at Starbucks stores nationwide, with five free items that customers can add to their drinks and food after making a purchase. According to the chain, when combined with the customisation options already available when ordering, the bar creates up to 5.27 million possible combinations.

The customisation bar is based on a concept seen at stores in the chain’s earlier days, when customers were able to freely add extras like milk, honey and cinnamon to their drinks. These bars were scaled back during the COVID-19 pandemic, but now Starbucks is reviving the concept on a larger scale, with two familiar favourites making a return alongside three new creations.

The two returning are: Honey, which is said to pair particularly well with the chain’s cappuccinos, and Cinnamon Powder, which goes well with a White Mocha, and any drink or food item topped with foam or whipped cream.

▼  The new offerings are Vanilla Sugar & Salt, Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce and Ginger Sugar Chips.

Vanilla Sugar & Salt combines pink salt flavoured with vanilla and granulated sugar, creating a sweet-and-salty flavour with a vanilla aroma that goes well with a Caramel Macchiato. Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce is a maple-flavoured sauce combined with black pepper and cardamom that’s said to pair well with both coffee and tea, and is particularly good in a Cafe Misto. Ginger Sugar Chips are small pieces of sugar combined with ginger, adding a subtle ginger flavour and a crunchy texture, and are recommended for a Coffee Frappuccino.

If the choices seem a little overwhelming, baristas are happy to share their favourite combinations, and Starbucks is sharing some top tips from three of its store employees.

▼ Global Barista Champion Nobuki Shimoide recommends combining a Caramel Macchiato with Vanilla Sugar & Salt.

The vanilla aroma and pink salt work well to bring out the caramel flavour while adding a sweet-and-savoury note reminiscent of salted caramel.

The chain’s “19th Coffee Ambassador”, Asumi Yamaguchi, recommends a Cappuccino topped with Cinnamon Powder and Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce.

This combination is said to highlight the sweetness of the milk while leaving a lingering spiciness on the palate.

Ayaka Okamoto, from Starbucks’ Ueno Onshi Park Store, suggests giving a Vanilla Cream Frappuccino a more grown-up twist with Ginger Sugar Chips and Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce.

The crunchy ginger sugar adds texture, while the maple sauce brings together the aromas of ginger, cardamom and black pepper.

Just reading those recommendations has us thirsty for a taste, and with the new options being free of charge, we can easily try them out on our next visit. Starbucks also says that special limited-edition seasonal releases may be added to the range in future, giving us even more ways to customise our orders without having to go through the potentially complicated process of explaining what we need to baristas behind the counter.

The My Customisation Bar will be introduced at Starbucks stores nationwide from 2 September.

Source, images: Press release

title: Ministop brings bulked up Okinawan-style rice balls to mainland Japan for one week only
description: If you’re craving massive meals on a budget, portion-boosted convenience store foods are the way to go. On the days that you forget to bring your lunch with you, or you’re simply too busy to prepare one, Japanese convenience stores are like an oasis in a desert of hunger. Yet, while the portion sizes are […]
content:
If you’re craving massive meals on a budget, portion-boosted convenience store foods are the way to go.

On the days that you forget to bring your lunch with you, or you’re simply too busy to prepare one, Japanese convenience stores are like an oasis in a desert of hunger. Yet, while the portion sizes are reasonable for those with a moderate appetite, if you’re one of those with a penchant for big eating, the popular convenience store trend of boosted sizes is a welcome endeavor. From August 25 until August 31, the second phase of Ministop’s Zukkyun Increased Portion Fair will run, featuring five items that are guaranteed to leave you feeling stuffed.

Rushing over to our nearest Ministop, we checked out the latest lineup:
1. Tuna Salad, Ham, and Egg Salad Sandwiches for 321 yen (US$2.02), with an additional Egg Sandwich.

2. Okinawa-style Pork and Egg Rice Ball (with Barley) for 321 yen, with double fillings.

3. Super Spicy Mapo Tofu and Spicy Fried Rice for 645 yen, with 50 percent increased volume.

4. Spaghetti with Garlic, Chili Peppers and Sausages (also known as the Sausage Peperoncino) for 572 yen, with over 50 percent more pasta and an extra sausage.

5. Infinite Cream for 321 yen, with a more than 50 percent increase in the amount of fresh whipped cream.

Starting with the Sausage Peperoncino, which felt the heaviest upon picking up, the weight turned out to be an incredible 604 grams (or 1.3 pounds).

The taste didn’t give us any surprises, being a fairly regular convenience store peperoncino, but the addition of one extra sausage was pleasant. Rather than having an obscure ingredient boosted, the sense of getting a good deal was very forthright.

Next up was the Mapo Tofu and Fried Rice, also being quite hefty at 540 grams (1.19 pounds).

While it doesn’t quite reach the “super spicy” level it claims to be, it still has a fairly solid kick, being at a level that some people might not be able to tolerate. So, if you’re not comfortable with the heat, it’s best to steer clear of this one.

The selection of sandwiches may just have one extra egg sandwich added, but it is pleasing in its simplicity.

Unfortunately, the store we went to didn’t have the Infinite Cream available, so we were unable to include it in our testing, despite our tongues longing for the sweet, velvety texture of the whipped cream.

For our top recommendation out of the entire lineup, it has to be the Okinawa-style Pork and Egg, which is absolutely packed with fillings.

Taking inspiration from the classic Okinawan food of the Spam Rice Ball (“Spam Musubi“), this rice ball is definitely one you should try, without even having to leave the mainland. The secret to this dish is how they’ve focused on increasing the fillings rather than the total weight, delivering a very high level of satisfaction and capable of satisfying a light hunger with just a single piece.

So, if your stomach wants to join in the extra food fun, the Okinawa-style Pork and Egg is recommended for overall satisfaction, but the Sausage Peperoncino is best for its cost-mass ratio. The number of items in Ministop’s fair might not be large, but they make for an enjoyable lunchtime.

title: Dragon Ball Z theme park, financed by Saudi Arabia, to be built in France
description: “You know of my interest in mangas,” says French president. It’s unusual for a single franchise to get an entire theme park of its own. Disneyland, of course, is a place for not only the Disney animated catalog, but also the various live-action properties the company now holds the rights to, such as Star Wars […]
content:
“You know of my interest in mangas,” says French president.

It’s unusual for a single franchise to get an entire theme park of its own. Disneyland, of course, is a place for not only the Disney animated catalog, but also the various live-action properties the company now holds the rights to, such as Star Wars and the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Universal Studios’ attractions cover a wide variety of Hollywood movies, plus Nintendo’s Super Mario and a handful of other video game and anime IPs. Even Ghibli Park is a place for the celebration of the studio’s overall output, not one specific film.

But there’s a dedicated Dragon Ball Z theme park on the way, though it’ll be opening on the opposite side of the hemisphere from the anime/manga’s home country.

The office of French president Emmanuel Macron has announced that a Dragon Ball Z theme park will be built in the suburbs of Paris. The facility will be one of three new theme parks to be developed in Cergy-Pontoise, roughly 45 minutes northwest of downtown Paris, which will ostensibly sit on the site of the former Mirapolis, an amusement park which closed in 1991.

This news might have jogged your memory that there’s also a Dragon Ball Z theme park in development in Saudi Arabia, and the French park will also be built with Saudi money. The three-park project, with a total budget of 6 billion Euros, (roughly US$7 billion), is being spearheaded by Qiddiya Investment Company, a Saudi government fund with crown prince and prime minister Mohammed bin Salman as its chairman. Talks for the French Dragon Ball Z park began a year and a half ago, when Macron and bin Salman found out they had a shared love for Dragon Ball Z, and the announcement of the French park was timed to coincide with bin Salman’s latest visit to Paris.

Posting to his official Twitter account, Macron said “You know of my interest in mangas. You are also aware of my determination to attract investments in France that will create employment and make the most ambitious projects possible,” while claiming that the parks will create 22,000 new jobs (for comparison, Oriental Land, the company that manages Tokyo Disneyland, Disney Sea, and its associated hotels, currently employs around 27,000 people). Macron expressed his gratitude with “Thank you to Qiddiya and to Saudi Arabia for your confidence in our country, our talents, and our future.”

As for when that Dragon Ball Z-ified future is coming, there’s currently no timetable for the Franch park’s opening, but given the size of the project, it’s probably going to be at least a few years until it’s ready to start receiving guests, which should give Macron more time to practice his Kamehameha pose.

Source: Jiji, Asahi Shimbun, Reuters, Oriental Land Company, Twitter/@EmmanuelMacron

title: Japan tripled its departure tax to fund tourism but is using the money on cherry blossoms and bears
description: Questions are being raised over whether money from foreign tourists is being used as intended. On 1 July, Japan increased its departure tax for everyone flying out of the country, raising it from 1,000 yen (US$6.28) to 3,000 yen per departure, with the cost included in the price of the airfare. While the threefold increase […]
content:
Questions are being raised over whether money from foreign tourists is being used as intended.

On 1 July, Japan increased its departure tax for everyone flying out of the country, raising it from 1,000 yen (US$6.28) to 3,000 yen per departure, with the cost included in the price of the airfare. While the threefold increase applies to both foreign tourists and Japanese citizens, the government acknowledged that most of the additional revenue would be collected from overseas visitors, estimating they would contribute around 646 billion yen (US$4.05 billion) this year, compared to roughly 164 billion yen from Japanese citizens.

To soften the blow, the government told the public that the extra revenue would go back into travel-related initiatives, like lowering passport fees for Japanese citizens, and funding programs to combat overtourism, including the promotion of lesser-known parts of Japan. However, it was revealed this week that the 2026 fiscal budget, which was approved in April before the higher departure tax came into effect, also allocated departure tax revenue to cover the costs of bear control and pest prevention for cherry blossom trees – measures that are largely aimed at protecting the lives and environment of people living in Japan rather than improving the experience of foreign visitors.

According to Japanese media reports, the government allocated 6.2 billion yen for bear-related countermeasures in the 2026 fiscal year, with 6 billion yen of that amount coming from departure tax revenue. A newly created 600 million-yen budget for pest control of sakura trees is reportedly being funded entirely by the departure tax.

The Environment Ministry has justified the spending, saying that foreign visitors could benefit from countermeasures against bears, and many people from abroad come to Japan specifically to see the cherry blossoms.

▼ Foreign tourists aren’t the only people who enjoy the blossoms, though, as locals flock to see them too.

Bear encounters have become an increasingly serious issue in Japan, with both local residents and foreign tourists sustaining injuries from the animals, including at tourist spots. However, after news of the allocations came to light this week, questions have been raised over whether the heavy funding of bear and sakura pest control aligns with the original intention of the increased tax, which was introduced to fund tourism-related initiatives.

It’s also important to note that bear control and cherry blossom tree pest prevention measures had traditionally been funded from the government’s general budget, which draws on taxes such as income and corporate tax without being restricted to a particular use. Those defending the new funding argue that money from the general budget can now be used to cover other costs, but it’s unclear where the resulting funds will be redirected.

In light of these revelations, and amid growing concerns from the public, Japan’s Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, Yasushi Kaneko, announced on 25 August that the government would consider reviewing how the money is allocated. He said the government would examine the spending carefully and work to ensure the money is directed towards projects with greater effectiveness and without raising concerns.

With tourism-related initiatives covering such a broad spectrum of issues that affect everyday life in Japan, it’s quite possible for the government to justify any use of funds if it has the slightest connection to tourism. As the government aims to increase the number of annual foreign visitors from over 40 million in 2025 to 60 million by 2030, the revenue collected from the departure tax is set to rise with it, making responsible use of funds even more vital to ensuring that the problems of overtourism don’t get lost amid concerns over sakura pests and bears.

Sources: Asahi Shimbun (1, 2) via Yahoo! News Japan (1, 2)

title: Amid foreign sex tourist rise, Japanese government considering outlawing paying for prostitution

content:
No selling should also mean no buying, expert panel says.

Common sense would suggest that if there’s something that’s been judged as unacceptable enough within a society for there to be a blanket ban on its sale, that buying it should be illegal too, right? Like, if the law says that “Under no circumstances can Godzilla eggs be sold,” it doesn’t seem like there’s any logical scenario in which it would be OK to purchase them.

And yet, in one of the many ways that Godzilla eggs and sexual intercourse are different, the Japanese legal system doesn’t handle buying sex the same as it does selling sex, as one is explicitly outlawed, and the other carries no legal penalty whatsoever. That loophole could be closing soon, though, and foreign tourists might be playing a role in the proposed revision.

Under Japan’s current Prostitution Prevention Law, only the selling of intercourse is treated as a criminal act. So if Person A pays Person B for a role in the hay, Person B is looking at up to six months in jail or a fine of up to 20,000 yen (US$125) if they get caught. Meanwhile, Person A hasn’t broken any law, and therefore faces no legal repercussion as long as they didn’t commit any other wrongdoing (such as sex with a minor, coercion, or physical assault).

As we discussed earlier this year, the Japanese government’s Ministry of Justice has come to feel like this imbalance is both unfair and ineffective, and assembled a panel of experts to discuss what changes need to be made. This week, the panel previewed its recommendations in a draft report, in which it says the members are in consensus that prostitution purchasers should be punished as well.

The proposal follows recent attempts by Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward to reduce prostitution within its section of the city, which includes the Kabukicho entertainment and red light district. Since the end of the pandemic, there’s been a noticeable increase in the number of streetwalkers on roads near a park and love hotel district close to Shinjuku Station. Ward administrators say that social media videos showing women loitering on the streets as they wait for customers looking to purchase sex have been attracting increasing amounts of attention overseas, leading to an increase in foreign tourists coming to the area to purchase the prostitutes’ services themselves or to gawk at the selection on display. In response, local citizens’ groups have begun public awareness patrols broadcasting announcements that “Prostitution is a crime” in both Japanese and English.

Though not the sole impetus for the proposed revisions, an unwanted increase in foreign sex tourists is one more reason to tighten the law. In addition to introducing penalties for purchasers, some on the panel also recommend raising the penalties for selling sex, saying that the current penalties are insufficient to dissuade prostitutes from offering their services. At the same time, the panel recognizes that increased penalties could carry the risk of driving prostitution further underground, increasing the dangers faced by those working within the industry if they feel unable to come forward to the police if customers or controllers become violent, and that efforts should be made to help those who see prostitution as their only means of making a living to obtain the economic and social support they need to transition to more lawful occupations.

The panel’s final report could be completed as soon as next month, which would allow legislation to criminalize paying for prostitution as early as the next session of the Diet (Japanese parliament), which is slated to start in late September.

Source: Yomiuri Shimbun (1, 2), Jiji
